newsitem.title: USA: N. Ireland fugitives fight extradition in U.S court.
newsitem.headline: N. Ireland fugitives fight extradition in U.S court.

text.p: A fugitive from a Northern Ireland prison was convicted in a "trumped-up case" and would face prejudice because of his political and religious beliefs if sent back, his lawyer said on Tuesday.

Attorney James Brosnahan made the charges at the start of a trial in a San Francisco courtroom to decide whether to grant a British request to extradite his client, Kevin Artt, and another fugitive, Terry Kirby.
Artt and Kirby were among 38 prisoners who escaped from Northern Ireland's Maze prison in 1983. Artt was arrested in June 1992 in San Diego and Kirby was arrested near San Francisco in 1994.

Another Maze escapee, Jimmy Smyth, was extradited in August after losing a four-year legal battle to stay in the United States. A fourth fugitive arrested on the U.S. West coast, Pol Brennan, is awaiting his extradition hearing.
Opening arguments and testimony on Tuesday focused on Artt, 38, who was serving a life sentence in Northern Ireland for the November 1978 murder of prison guard Albert Miles.

The trial, before U.S. District Judge Charles Legge, is expected to last about four weeks and will include testimony from witnesses who have travelled from Northern Ireland and others who gave videotaped depositions.

Brosnahan said Artt was convicted in a "trumped-up case" and did not murder Miles. He said Artt signed a confession typed by police after five days of interrogation in 1981 and that was the only evidence against him.

Brosnahan said Artt was an "IRA wannabe" -- referring to Irish Republican Army guerrillas fighting to end British rule in Northern Ireland -- but said Artt never joined and was acquitted of IRA membership by a Northern Ireland judge.

Artt would suffer prejudice because of his religious and political beliefs if extradited, Brosnahan said. "We will ask you to find that Mr. Artt should not be returned under the treaty to Northern Ireland," he told the judge.
Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Zanides, representing the British government, denied the murder case against Artt was "trumped-up" and said he would not be mistreated if sent back.

He said Artt, a taxi driver, came to the attention of Northern Ireland security forces between 1978 and 1981 because he was involved in driving away three people from a "kneecapping," in which a man had his knee blown off.

Brosnahan told Legge he wanted to see the Stalker report, the confidential report of a British inquiry into allegations that Northern Ireland police operated a shoot-to-kill policy. The British government refused to hand over the document when requested to do so during the Smyth case.
The hearing will later hear evidence about Kirby, who was also serving a life sentence for murder when he escaped.

The Smyth case was the first test of a recent amendment to the U.S.-British extradition treaty that said U.S. courts may refuse to extradite anyone who would be persecuted because of their race, religion or political beliefs if returned. A U.S. District judge initially denied Smyth's extradition, ruling he would be punished for his political opinions, but the decision was overturned on appeal.
